Title: Slice Agent: Identifying and Isolating Slices in Shared Open Radio Unit

Open Radio Unit

Abstract
Network Slice as a Service (NSaaS) is a key enabler of Beyond Fifth Gener-
ation (5G) and Sixth Generation (6G) networks, supporting next-generation
applications such as extended reality (XR), immersive services, and the tac-
tile Internet. These networks must provide native support for slice-aware
services across the entire Radio Access Network (RAN), including the Ra-
dio Unit (RU), Distributed Unit (DU), Central Unit (CU), and transport
segments (fronthaul, midhaul, and backhaul). However, uplink slicing iden-
tification in shared Open-RUs (O-RUs) presents a fundamental challenge
because the Open-DU (O-DU) handles scheduling, and the O-RU does not
inherently know which uplink data belongs to which slice. In MultiPoint-to-
MultiPoint (MP2MP) fronthaul scenarios, this limitation is further exacer-
bated by synchronization and timing constraints, which necessitate that the
O-RU process control messages and the encapsulated data be delivered with
ultra-low latency. To address this issue, we propose a slicing agent embedded
in the O-RU that identifies slices and segregates uplink data into slice-specific
enhanced Common Public Radio Interface (eCPRI) packets. Our design em-
ploys a pipeline architecture with dedicated paths for time-sensitive, flexible
slicing, enabling slice isolation and prioritization. When implemented on an
Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), the agent processes each packet in
2 clock cycles, supporting up to 3822 slices per slot. Experimental results val-
idate the approach, showing its feasibility, scalability, and high-performance

1. Introduction
Fifth Generation (5G) mobile networks have adopted new technologies,
such as network slicing and disaggregated Radio Access Network (RAN),
to deliver services with different requirements, including Enhanced Mobile
Broadband (eMBB), Ultra-Reliable Low Latency Communications (URLLC),
and massive Machine-Type Communications (mMTC) [1]. At first, mobile
operators used network slices in a static way because there were only a few
slices, and orchestration methods were new. As demand for specialized ser-
vices and Zero-Touch Network and Service Management (ZSM) increased, re-
search and open-source efforts began to enable dynamic network slicing. Eu-
ropean Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) forecasts that soon,
Network Slice as a Service (NSaaS) will be provided across several domains,
including RAN, transport, and core networks [2]. In Beyond 5G and Sixth
Generation (6G) networks, NSaaS is expected to be a key, built-in part of
the system, enabling End-to-End (E2E) service access for new use cases such
as immersive experiences, extended reality, and the tactile Internet [2].
Disaggregated RANs were conceptualized more than ten years ago, di-
viding the monolithic Distributed RAN (D-RAN) into Remote Radio Heads
(RRHs) and Baseband Units (BBUs) to reduce costs and enhance Quality
of Service (QoS) for mobile operators [3]. A centralized BBU pool gave rise
to Cloud-RAN, leveraging cloud computing principles. The Third Gener-
ation Partnership Project (3GPP) introduced a novel segmentation in Re-
lease 15 [4], further refined in Releases 16 [5] and 17 [6], by dividing the
RAN into three elements: Radio Unit (RU), Distributed Unit (DU), and
Central Unit (CU). While such functional splits and partial disaggregation
are already present in current 5G deployments, their large-scale openness,
full programmability, and tight integration with slicing mechanisms are still
evolving. The Open RAN (O-RAN) ALLIANCE was established to create
open interfaces for the cohesive operation of these elements, independent of
vendors, and to facilitate the development of new services and applications
[7]. In this context, Beyond 5G and 6G networks are expected to extend and
2


consolidate these disaggregation principles, incorporating native support for
NSaaS and programmable RAN architectures, tightly integrating slice ser-
vices with the RU, DU, and CU, as well as with fronthaul, midhaul, and
backhaul transport connections.
In the O-RAN architecture, the chosen Lower Layer Split (LLS) aims
to propose a good trade-off between the required bandwidth and the com-
plexity of the O-RU, reducing costs [8]. From the O-RAN specifications,
Open-DU (O-DU) and Open-CU (O-CU) already support slicing, but not
Open-RU (O-RU) [9]. Slicing support adds functionality to the O-RU, and
maintaining a relatively low cost remains challenging. These LLSs become
more challenging when the shared O-RU and multipoint-to-multipoint fron-
thaul scenario is considered, as new challenges involving synchronization and
slice identification must be addressed [10]. The main challenge in identifying
slices within the O-RU lies in the uplink process, because the O-RU does
not know which data should be sent to the O-DU, as it is the O-DU that
performs the scheduling process [7]. In this context, the O-RU must receive
precise uplink scheduling information in advance, enabling it to associate the
received signals from User Equipments (UEs) with the corresponding slices,
encapsulate them, and forward them to the appropriate O-DU. This process
is subject to strict time constraints, requiring the O-RU to be synchronized
with other network components and to process scheduling information within
a short time window [8].
We propose an architecture for slicing identification and segregation in the
uplink process, addressing this challenge directly within the O-RU, denoted
Slice Agent.
Our proposal uses the existing O-RAN fronthaul to receive
slice information and encapsulate radio data into separate Ethernet packets
for each slice. Additionally, it designs two processing units to enable slice
isolation and prioritization. Moreover, we present an experimental case to
evaluate the performance of the Slice Agent. The main contributions of this
work are:
(i) We present Slice Agent, an architecture designed to enable slicing sup-
port in the uplink process within the O-RU.
(ii) We introduce a pipeline and parallel architecture to achieve high per-
formance in slicing identification.
(iii) We demonstrate high processing capacity, capable of handling the max-
imum theoretical load in specific scenarios.
3


(iv) We develop a simulation environment to validate Slice Agent and carry
out scalability tests using the real prototype.
The results demonstrate the feasibility and high performance of the pro-
posed architecture for real-time, slice-aware uplink processing. By leveraging
a pipeline design with dedicated paths for time-sensitive, flexible RAN slic-
ing, the Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA)-based implementation can
process each packet in 2 clock cycles, achieving ultra-low latency. The sys-
tem supports up to 3,822 slices per slot across two slicing types, including
URLLC and eMBB, demonstrating substantial scalability under demanding
traffic conditions.
Experimental validation confirms the approach’s effec-
tiveness, highlighting its potential to enable efficient, programmable slicing
mechanisms in Beyond 5G and 6G networks.
The article is structured as follows: Section 2 covers the study’s essential
concepts. Section 3 discusses previous research on slicing support in RUs and
fronthaul. Section 4 details the Slice Agent architecture. Section 5 outlines
the prototype implementation and provides an experimental case study to
evaluate the performance of the proposed architecture.
Lastly, Section 6
concludes the article and outlines future directions.
2. Background
This section presents fundamental concepts regarding RANs and their
relevant characteristics as applicable to this article. First, the basic architec-
ture of a mobile network is given, followed by a brief explanation of RAN,
with a focus on its disaggregation. Finally, the concept of network slicing is
introduced.
Mobile network
Mobile cellular networks constitute the foundation of contemporary wire-
less communications, supporting a wide range of services. A cellular network
architecture is traditionally structured into three main components: the Core
Network, RAN, and UE. The Core Network, typically deployed in operators’
data centers, is responsible for essential control and user-plane functions, in-
cluding authentication, mobility management, session establishment, and ex-
ternal network connectivity. RAN provides the wireless interface between the
UE and the Core, performing radio signal processing, resource management,
4


and protocol stack functions required to ensure reliable and efficient commu-
nication. UE refers to the end devices accessing the network, encompassing
smartphones and Internet of Things (IoT) terminals [11, 12, 13].
This architecture has continuously evolved across successive generations,
driven by increasingly stringent requirements for data rate, latency, relia-
bility, and service diversity. In this context, 5G has reached a mature de-
ployment stage worldwide, with current efforts primarily focused on perfor-
mance optimization, network automation, and the support of heterogeneous
services. At the same time, research initiatives and early standardization
activities have increasingly shifted toward defining 6G, aiming to address
emerging requirements and extend the architectural foundations established
by 5G [14, 15].
Radio Access Network
RAN is a critical component of 5G networks, connecting UEs, such as
smartphones, to the Core Network and enabling wireless communication and
data exchange.
In earlier generations of mobile networks, the RAN was
typically implemented as a monolithic entity, with radio frequency, baseband
processing, and control functionalities tightly integrated into a single vendor-
dependent device. With the evolution of cellular systems, particularly during
the Long Term Evolution (LTE) era, the first steps toward architectural dis-
aggregation were introduced through the separation of radio and baseband
functions. This disaggregation led to the emergence of Cloud-RAN architec-
tures, in which the radio functionality was implemented by RRHs deployed
near the antennas, while the BBUs were centralized to enable resource pool-
ing and coordination. Subsequent advances in network virtualization further
enabled the BBU to be a software-based entity running on cloud infrastruc-
tures [16, 17]. Building upon these developments, the stringent and heteroge-
neous requirements introduced by 5G, including low latency, high data rates,
and massive connectivity, have driven the adoption of more flexible and scal-
able RAN architectures. In this context, the RAN has evolved toward a fully
disaggregated model, formally structured into CU, DU, and RU, where the
CU and DU conceptually extend the traditional BBU, and the RU represents
the evolution of the RRH [18].
In the context of 5G, functional splits are crucial. Functional splits refer
to how the RAN’s processing tasks are divided among the CU, DU, and
RU. Therefore, the choice of split impacts the complexity of each unit and
the bandwidth and latency requirements for each network segment.
The
5


3GPP, which defines global telecommunications standards, introduced eight
functional split options, each tailored to different network requirements and
deployment scenarios.
The High Layer Split (HLS), which separates the CU and DU, was defined
by 3GPP as Option 2 and is considered to offer the best cost-benefit ratio.
This split balances processing capabilities and network efficiency, making it
a widely adopted standard in 5G deployments. On the other hand, the LLS,
which separates the DU and RU, was not explicitly defined by 3GPP. This
decision was made because the optimal choice for the LLS depends heavily on
specific applications and deployment scenarios. As a result, different industry
groups have proposed various options for this split, such as Split 6 by the
Small Cell Forum (SCF) and Split 7.2x by the O-RAN Alliance, each tailored
to meet the distinct needs of 5G networks [19]. Figure 1 presents an overview
of the division of the New Radio protocol into CU, DU, and RU in several
architectures.

The disaggregation of the RAN into CU, DU, and RU introduces new
interfaces within the network. The backhaul is the interface between the CU
6


and the Core network, ensuring connectivity and communication between the
RAN and the network’s central components. The midhaul is the interface
between the CU and DU, while the fronthaul is the interface between the
DU and RU. These interfaces are fundamental to maintaining the flexibility
and scalability of 5G networks, enabling operators to optimize the placement
and operation of each RAN component for specific use cases and deployment
scenarios [20].
Network slicing
Network slicing constitutes one of the architectural pillars of 5G, enabling
the deployment of multiple logically isolated networks over a shared physi-
cal infrastructure. Instead of statically partitioning resources, slicing allows
operators to dynamically tailor connectivity profiles according to heteroge-
neous service demands, including throughput, latency, reliability, and isola-
tion requirements [21, 22]. This concept introduces significant orchestration
complexity, since diverse service instances must coexist while competing for
common computational, transport, and radio resources. However, once this
complexity is addressed, network slicing enables operators to allocate net-
work resources more efficiently and deliver customized services to different
user types and applications.
From a standardization perspective, the slicing framework defined by
3GPP establishes the concept of a Network Slice Instance (NSI), whose lifecy-
cle is managed through dedicated management functions such as the Network
Slice Management Function (NSMF) [23]. Building upon this foundation,
the O-RAN Alliance integrates slicing support into its service management
and orchestration layer through the Service Management and Orchestra-
tion (SMO), extending slice management capabilities to an E2E approach
[9, 24]. Complementarily, the IETF specifies a non-prescriptive reference ar-
chitecture for network slicing in which customer requests for Network Slice
Services are handled by a Network Slice Controller (NSC), establishing a
common framework that promotes interoperability and conceptual alignment
across diverse slicing implementations [25].
The E2E slicing nature is a fundamental requirement for this paradigm,
since a slice must not be confined to a single domain but span the 5G Core
(5GC), the Transport Network (TN), the RAN, and ultimately the UE. Such
E2E continuity ensures that performance guarantees are consistently enforced
throughout the entire communication path, thereby enabling Service Level
Agreement (SLA) compliance across heterogeneous network segments [12,
7


13]. Consequently, all involved domains must support slice-aware control,
monitoring, and resource isolation mechanisms.
Slice identification and traffic differentiation rely on standardized identi-
fiers. For each operator, uniquely defined by the Public Land Mobile Net-
work IDentifier (PLMN-ID), slice selection during Protocol Data Unit (PDU)
session establishment is performed using the Single Network Slice Selec-
tion Assistance Information (S-NSSAI), which comprises the Slice Service
Type (SST) and the Slice Differentiator (SD) [9]. This mechanism allows
multiple slices to coexist within the same public land mobile network while
maintaining traffic separation and QoS assurance. In the TN, PDU sessions
are transported over Ethernet-based infrastructures [26], and operators must
correlate session flows with their corresponding NSIs to preserve isolation
and performance differentiation. Moreover, slicing supports multi-operator
deployments through RAN sharing scenarios. Thanks to functional disag-
gregation and open interfaces, infrastructure components, potentially from
different vendors, can be shared among multiple operators while maintaining
slice-level separation [9]. This capability significantly enhances the flexibility
of infrastructure utilization and deployment.
Beyond static slice provisioning, the slicing paradigm is evolving toward
a service-oriented model commonly referred to as NSaaS. In this approach,
slices are instantiated, scaled, and terminated on demand, similarly to cloud-
native services. Such a model enables vertical industries and enterprise cus-
tomers to request customized connectivity solutions aligned with specific
business objectives, requiring advanced automation, programmability, and
lifecycle management across orchestration frameworks [27]. The realization
of NSaaS therefore depends on tight integration between slice management
functions, virtualization platforms, and standardization for all architectural
domains.
3. Related work
Several studies have explored tools to support slicing in 5G networks.
However, there is a noticeable gap in the studied technology, particularly
regarding slicing support directly by the RU [20, 28]. The survey presented by
Arnhold et al. [20] provides a detailed review of the work in this field, which
identified opportunities that have led to the development of the technology
presented in this article. In this context, some existing work addresses this
concept, primarily focusing on fronthaul.
8


The 5G Crosshaul project [29, 30, 31] defines an architecture for a 5G
network that supports crosshaul, characterized by the coexistence of back-
haul, midhaul, and fronthaul interfaces within a single physical network. For
this coexistence to be achieved, the system must inherently support net-
work slicing to ensure traffic isolation. In the fronthaul case, where slicing
identification is unavailable, slicing support was provided by dedicated net-
work elements deployed within the transport network between devices, en-
abling proper traffic routing and prioritization. Under this approach, new
and customized transport elements will be required, increasing the cost of
the network infrastructure. A slicing technology provided directly by an RU
eliminates the need for such additional elements, allowing the use of existing
infrastructure. This approach enables the RU to manage multiple slices inde-
pendently, simplifying the network architecture and reducing the complexity
associated with routing and split selection. By integrating slicing capabilities
directly into the RU, it is possible to support diverse slices within a shared
RU scenario, leveraging existing infrastructure without requiring significant
modifications or additional network components.
The Sliced RAN project [32, 33] also presents an interesting proposal
to support slicing E2E. In this case, the fronthaul is designed to support
multiple slices, ensuring each slice receives sufficient bandwidth. This objec-
tive is achieved by determining the optimal routing path across the available
network elements and selecting the optimal functional split for each slice.
However, this project assumes that an RU can serve only one DU, limiting
its applicability in scenarios involving a shared RU. In such cases, where a
single RU is expected to support multiple slices originating from different
DUs, this project falls short, making it unsuitable for the shared RU use
case.
In the New Radio protocol, for a downlink or uplink transmission to
occur, it must first be scheduled by the scheduling algorithm running in
the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer within the DU.
This schedul-
ing process provides advanced knowledge of downlink and uplink informa-
tion, enabling informed decisions and reducing latency.
The Cooperative
Dynamic Bandwidth Allocation (CO-DBA) is an International Telecommu-
nication Union (ITU) standard-supported technique (G.Suppl.71) that re-
duces upstream latency in Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM)-Passive Op-
tical Networks (PONs), particularly for 5G mobile fronthaul [34]. In this
case, CO-DBA calculates the necessary bandwidth required by PONs to per-
form downlink and uplink transmissions for a specific slice [35]. CO-DBA
9


can determine the required bandwidth by obtaining scheduling information
in advance, even before the actual data transfer begins, reducing latency and
supporting low-latency applications, a key goal of beyond 5G and 6G net-
works. Several works utilize the CO-DBA technology, as presented by Uzawa
et al. [35], which proposed a CO-DBA algorithm for a time-division multi-
plex PON. In this work, the time interval is divided into multiple grant cycles
to ensure guaranteed bandwidth allocation. These grant cycle divisions are
done using the scheduling information received in advance. The same con-
cept is used by Das et al. [36, 37, 38, 39] and Mondal and Rufini [40]. In
all cases, the CO-DBA is used to ensure bandwidth allocation to slicing with
different requirements in a low-latency scenario. However, the shared RU use
case, in which a single RU supports multiple slices from different DUs, is not
addressed by this approach, leaving a gap in current technology.
Budhdev et al.
[41] used a similar technique to identify a slice.
The
authors proposed a method implemented in a programmable switch that
receives scheduling information in advance, enabling accurate identification
and forwarding of incoming data packets. The focus was on the uplink pro-
cedure, as the RU lacked information about the incoming data. However,
programmable switches are costly, and in a complex RAN with interface co-
existence and multiple RUs and DUs, synchronization between all transport
elements poses a significant challenge. In fact, synchronization across fron-
thaul transport elements is a challenge in disaggregated and multipoint RAN
architectures, affecting not only the solution proposed by Budhdev et al., but
also any approaches that require tight timing coordination among RUs, DUs,
and transport components.
In the current specifications of the O-RAN Alliance regarding the fron-
thaul, the focus is primarily on functional disaggregation and the definition
and consolidation of an open interface, namely Open Fronthaul, between
the O-DU and the O-RU, as described in the latest release of the Work
Group 4 (WG4) Control, User, and Synchronization Plane (CUS) specifica-
tions [42]. WG4 is the main initiative within the O-RAN architecture for
Open Fronthaul. The document released by this group spans over 500 pages
and provides detailed specifications for architecture, transport, security, and
the control, user, and synchronization planes. However, despite this level of
detail, support for network slicing is not explicitly addressed at the fronthaul
level.
The O-RAN Alliance’s vision of network slicing has evolved incremen-
tally, reflecting the broader goal of extending slicing capabilities beyond the
10


core network and logical RAN functions into the transport domain. This
evolution is more clearly articulated in Work Group 1 (WG1), which defines
the slicing architecture, use cases, and requirements for O-RAN systems [43].
In particular, slicing is treated as an E2E concept, encompassing core, RAN,
and transport segments. However, a clear mismatch emerges between these
two perspectives. While WG1 defines slicing as an E2E characteristic, the
fronthaul specifications in WG4 lack explicit mechanisms to support slice-
aware transport. As a result, slicing in the fronthaul is implicitly assumed to
rely on traditional QoS differentiation and traffic prioritization mechanisms,
rather than on native slice identification and isolation.
This limitation becomes even more critical in emerging deployment sce-
narios, such as neutral-host and multi-operator RANs, where a common
physical infrastructure must support multiple tenants with distinct service
requirements. Within this context, the use cases defined by WG4, especially
Use Case 7 (multi-slice support) and Use Case 10 (multi-operator and multi-
vendor scenarios), foresee that a single O-RU will simultaneously serve mul-
tiple slices and multiple O-DUs [43, 42]. This capability inherently requires
slice-aware traffic handling in the fronthaul transport plane. Therefore, a key
challenge arises from the absence of native slice identifiers in current Open
Fronthaul transport protocols, such as eCPRI. While the 3GPP defines slice
identifiers, such as S-NSSAI, at the system level [12, 13], these identifiers are
not directly available at the fronthaul transport layer. This specification cre-
ates a gap between the slice definition and the slice deployment, particularly
in the transport segment closest to the O-RU.
To overcome this limitation, current discussions point toward the need
for mapping higher-layer slice-related information, such as PLMN-ID or QoS
profiles, into transport-level identifiers. One promising approach leverages
Ethernet-based mechanisms, such as VLAN tagging (IEEE 802.1Q), priority
code points (PCP), and, in some cases, IP/UDP flow descriptors, to differ-
entiate traffic from distinct slices. By mapping PLMN-ID or slice-related
attributes to VLAN IDs and associated priority levels, it becomes possible to
enforce traffic separation across both user and control planes in the fronthaul.
Therefore, the lack of explicit slice-aware mechanisms in the fronthaul rep-
resents a fundamental limitation for achieving true E2E network slicing. In
particular, it can become a bottleneck for strict QoS enforcement, especially
in latency-sensitive applications such as industrial automation and mission-
critical communications [44]. This gap underscores the need for mechanisms
that bring slice awareness into the fronthaul transport domain.

In the following, we analyze the related work from a comparative per-
spective across three architectural dimensions: crosshaul capability, trans-
port specialization requirements, and support for MP2MP connectivity. This
structured comparison highlights common design assumptions and clarifies
the architectural positioning of the proposed Slice Agent. Table 1 presents a
comparison of the related work. Most proposals support a crosshaul network.
For example, the 5G Crosshaul project [29, 30, 31] achieved the state-of-the-
art with a packet-oriented network. These solutions used techniques such as
Virtual Local Area Network (VLAN) and Internet Protocol (IP) to identify
and isolate each interface.
Additionally, other works utilized optical net-
works, which can support multiple domains by isolating them in the time
and frequency domains. Since the proposed Slice Agent uses the O-RAN
fronthaul architecture, which is also a packet-oriented network, it is possi-
ble to support multiple interfaces on the same network, isolating each with
VLANs, as in other projects. However, the proposals by Budhdev et al. [41]
and the Sliced RAN project [32, 33] considered only fronthaul data, limit-
ing their functionality to a single transport interface and not supporting a
complete crosshaul network.
Most existing studies focus on the transport domain and rely on spe-
cialized transport elements, which increases overall network complexity. For
instance, in the 5G Crosshaul project, specialized routers handle fronthaul
routing. In [35], a dedicated Dynamic Bandwidth Allocation (DBA) must
be implemented within an optical element, and in the EAST-WEST PON
architecture, a specialized optical router enables dynamic horizontal-plane
routing rather than the traditional north-south routing. Similarly, Mondal
and Ruffini [40] developed a custom server to facilitate data exchange be-
tween two PON stages. The use of programmable switches by Budhdev [41]
increased the implementation’s cost and complexity, requiring a distinct al-
gorithm on each network switch. However, the proposed Slice Agent system
enables slicing identification and isolation at the RU, which assigns VLANs
to designate routes, allowing the use of commercial switches with VLAN
capabilities to interface with RAN elements.
Ojaghi et al.
[32, 33] used
the same approach, in which the fronthaul model relies on simple transport
elements. In the shared RU context, only the proposed Slice Agent is capa-
ble of handling this task. By using scheduling information in advance, the
Slice Agent is designed to separate the RU data into several packets, each of
which can be directed to a different DU. By identifying these packets with
a VLAN, the transport switching elements can forward the data along the
12


correct path. Although the approaches proposed by Ojaghi et al. [32, 33]
support dynamic reconfiguration of links between elements, they assume a
single RU-to-DU connection, thus preventing one RU from simultaneously
serving multiple DUs.
As a third comparison dimension, we examine support for MP2MP archi-
tectures. Related work based on packet-switched architectures [29, 30, 31,
32, 33, 41] inherently enables MultiPoint-to-MultiPoint (MP2MP) connec-
tivity. The specialized WEST-EAST PON architecture [36, 37, 38, 39] also
supports this characteristic. In this architecture, a dedicated optical router
is defined, making it possible to reroute the optical signal to a same-level ele-
ment. Even if the signal is directed to a specific point, the mesh architecture
enables dynamic routing, allowing changes not only to the paths but also to
the elements connected to them. The DBA scheme in [35] is an algorithm
specifically designed for the Optical Line Terminal (OLT) element in a PON,
supporting a one-to-n connection rather than a MP2MP setup. The pro-
posed Slice Agent leverages packet switching to interconnect multiple RAN
elements via the fronthaul.

The state-of-the-art review reveals that slicing identification and isola-
tion are not performed by the RU, and that current techniques focus on the
transport domain. This approach increases the cost of transport elements
and necessitates specific support for slicing. Transferring slice identification
to the RU offers significant benefits to the overall architecture. First, the
RU already includes specialized processors, such as Application-Specific In-
tegrated Circuits (ASICs) and FPGAs, so adding slicing identification would
have minimal impact on the RU’s design. Second, by performing slice identifi-
cation directly at the RU, slice-aware information can be explicitly embedded
13


into fronthaul packets, enabling transport switches to apply prioritization,
traffic engineering, and QoS policies in MP2MP scenarios without requiring
complex per-flow inspection mechanisms. In this way, transport elements
remain slice-aware while leveraging standardized mechanisms for differenti-
ated forwarding. Finally, use cases, such as a shared RU and multiple paths
between RU and DU, can be dynamically arranged. In this article, we pro-
pose the Slice Agent within the RU, responsible for identifying the slicing
and segregating RU data into packets for each slice. The following sections
describe the proposed architecture.
4. Slice Agent architecture
This section introduces the Slice Agent architecture and explains how
it achieves slicing identification and RU data segregation.
We begin this
description with key decisions, followed by an overview of the proposed ar-
chitecture. Finally, we detail each block of the proposed architecture.
Key decisions
The choice of the LLS fundamentally defines the fronthaul performance
requirements, as it determines the functional split between O-RU and O-DU,
specifying which 5G New Radio (NR) Physical Layer (PHY) processing func-
tions are executed at each unit. This architectural decision directly impacts
latency, throughput, synchronization accuracy, and implementation cost. In
this context, the O-RAN architecture is a trend due to its openness and the
selection of the LLS. O-RAN uses the functional split option 7.2x between
O-RU and O-DU, where only the low PHY functions of the NR are per-
formed by the O-RU. This split enables dynamic bandwidth in the fronthaul
with a significantly lower-cost RU. Moreover, O-RAN specifies the fronthaul,
providing tools to enable communication between O-DU and O-RU in com-
pliance with the specifications, including separation of user, control, synchro-
nization, and management planes. Additionally, the fronthaul specification
is packet-switched, increasing its flexibility and optimization opportunities.
Considering this context, the proposed Slice Agent was developed within the
O-RAN architecture.
The biggest challenge in the scenario presented is identifying and segre-
gating fronthaul packets by the O-RU. The O-RU performs only low PHY,
meaning all scheduling and data identification functions are performed inside
the O-DU, i.e., the MAC layer. Taking into account the downlink flow, the
14


O-DU can efficiently pack New Radio data into tagged fronthaul packets,
since it has all the necessary information, including which slice each packet
belongs to and which O-RU packet it must be sent to the O-DU. However, in
the uplink flow, the O-RU does not implement the necessary mechanisms to
identify each slice and to pack the NR data with the correct tag. Moreover,
O-RAN does not specify in its documentation the support for slicing in the
fronthaul, although it does provide some tools to enable flow identification.
As uplink identification remains an open challenge, this project focuses solely
on the uplink process, operating within the O-RU process.

The second step performs scheduling data processing, transforming slice-
oriented information into symbol-oriented information, which is easier to
handle by encapsulation. This step comprises two units: one for slices that
must be processed as soon as scheduling information is received, identified as
slice type "1", and the other for slices for which the time between reception
and processing is not predefined, identified as slice type "2". Although only
two slice types are defined, multiple independent instances of each slice type
may coexist simultaneously in the system. The following section provides a
detailed explanation of both units, highlighting their key differences. These
units are responsible for assembling all packets to be transmitted per symbol,
maintaining slice-specific information, including the slice identification tag,
mapped to the VLAN and eAxC ID, and frequency allocation parameters

the 5G New Radio protocol.
The third step is responsible for encapsulating all packets prepared in the
previous step. Encapsulation is divided into three stages: (i) application,
(ii) transport, and (iii) Ethernet. The encapsulation of the application layer
reads the prepared information and assembles the application packet with
only the relevant In-phase/Quadrature (I/Q) symbols for the current slice.
The transport layer encapsulation adds the eCPRI header, and the Ethernet
encapsulation adds the Ethernet header with the VLAN tag attached. In
this case, the packet is completed and sent to the Ethernet transceiver. A
control unit is defined as the unit that controls everything. This unit commu-
nicates with the O-RU controller through the fronthaul management plane,
configures the Slice Agent, and controls the latch actions.
The pipeline structure
The design of the Slice Agent features a pipeline structure to optimize
the utilization of hardware resources on the FPGA. This design also reduces
processing time by enabling parallelization. Figure 4 presents a simplified
structure of the adopted pipeline, containing three stages. The first stages
represent decoding the C-plane message and processing the scheduling in-
formation. The process starts in the first stage when a packet arrives at
the Slice Agent. After the information is decoded, the second stage begins,
allowing the first stage to become free to receive a new C-plane message si-
multaneously. As there are two processing units, the second stage runs in
parallel. Finally, the third stage occurs based on the time slot change and
uses information generated by the second-stage run in the previous time slot.

C-Plane Message Decoding
O-RU must receive at least one scheduling message for each existing slice.
The C-Plane Message Decoding receives those messages and addresses them
to the correct processing unit, depending on the type configured for the
respective slice. The control message comprises details about the time and
frequency domains for a specific slice. In the time domain, it includes frame,
subframe, slot, and symbol information, while in the frequency domain, it
specifies the PRBs utilized on the given symbols.
The eAxC ID is extracted from the message as soon as the control mes-
sage is received.
Using this tag, the process consults the control unit to
determine whether the corresponding slice is present in the slice list, and
sends it to the appropriate processing unit. The control unit maintains the
slice list, and the decoding process consults it. If eAxC ID is in the control
unit list, the decoded data is sent to the type "1" processing unit. Otherwise,
the decoded data is sent to the type "2" unit. This design allows a reduced
list containing only the slices that must be processed immediately.
Scheduling data processing
After decoding the C-plane message, all the information is stored in a
buffer and read by the processing part.
Figure 5 presents the processing
unit for considered two types of units. They are very similar but differ in
how they handle scheduling information. While the Type "1" unit reads the
data sequentially, requiring only a simple buffer, the Type "2" unit must be
able to reinsert data into the C-plane buffer, as the information could be out
of order. The processing output consists of the packet parameters and the
symbols relevant to this packet. A demultiplexer at the output replicates
the data to the appropriate symbol buffers in parallel based on the selection
information calculated in the processing part.
To initiate processing, the slot information in the First In, First Out
(FIFO) output data must match the slot information received by the O-RU
synchronization module. This information includes the frame, subframe, and
slot identifiers for the next time slot. If this matches the slice information

received via control messages, uplink processing will occur in the next time
slot. The key difference in the Type "2" processing unit is how it handles
scheduling information from the input FIFO. If the information is not rel-
evant for the current time slot, it is popped from the FIFO and reinserted
at the FIFO input rather than blocking processing as in the Type "1" unit.
This approach increases flexibility at the expense of determinism. Depending
on the number of slices to be reinserted, this process may take longer and
consume more buffer memory.
Scheduling processing prepares the PRB data associated with each slice
for transmission in the upcoming NR slot. Each slice is characterized by
its allocated PRBs and corresponding symbol positions. Since an NR slot
consists of 14 OFDM symbols, 14 dedicated symbol buffers are maintained.
The demultiplexer directs the PRBs for each slice to the appropriate symbol
buffers based on the scheduling decision. Once organized per symbol, the
PRB data must be encapsulated into Ethernet packets for fronthaul trans-
mission. The maximum number of PRBs that can be included in a single
packet depends on the network MTU and on the size of each PRB, which
in turn is determined by configuration parameters such as numerology and
19


I/Q sample width. As a result, a slice may require multiple Ethernet packets
per slot. For each slice, the total number of required packets is computed
based on the number of allocated PRBs and the maximum PRB capacity
per packet. For example, Slice 1 (S1) contains 61 PRBs, divided into two
packets: one for PRBs 0 to 30 and another for PRBs 31 to 60. Additionally,
Slice 2 (S2) is shown to have 11 PRBs, requiring one packet per symbol.
The maximum number of slices depends on the O-RU bandwidth and
the adopted resource granularity. For instance, in the FR1 band, with O-RU
deployment with a bandwidth of 100 MHz (273 PRBs), and assuming symbol-
level slicing granularity, i.e., each PRB allocated per OFDM symbol is treated
as an independent slice, the theoretical upper bound becomes 273×14 = 3822
slices per slot. For µ = 1 (30 kHz subcarrier spacing), slot duration in 5G
NR is 0.5 ms with 14 symbols.
The proposed architecture was intentionally designed to operate at the
highest possible resource granularity, namely at the PRB-symbol level. This
design choice ensures maximum flexibility, allowing the slicing mechanism to
support both control-plane and data-plane transmissions. The symbol-level
implementation provides a structural upper bound and guarantees compat-
ibility with scenarios involving short-duration allocations, including control
signaling and future ultra-low-latency configurations, and enables forecasting
the feasibility of single-symbol transport blocks for 6G extremely low-latency
applications.

The packet information stored in the symbol buffers is not sorted by

mMTC use case
The mMTC scenario simulates a high-density network environment where
numerous small devices transmit data packets.
This use case focuses on

• URLLC slices marked as type "2": we created four slices with 30 PRBs

the width of the I/Q samples. Processing starts when the decoded C-plane

6. Conclusion
5G and forthcoming 6G systems introduce a paradigm shift in cellular
network design, driven by virtualization, disaggregation, and intelligence at
the RAN level. Within this context, O-RAN plays a central role by enabling
open interfaces and programmable components that support advanced func-
tionalities such as Network Slicing. While slicing is conceptually defined at
higher layers, its practical enforcement at the fronthaul level introduces non-
trivial architectural and hardware challenges, particularly within the O-RU,
where cost, latency, and processing constraints are critical.
This work proposed and implemented Slice Agent, a hardware-based slic-
ing support mechanism for the O-RU fronthaul. The proposed architecture
enables real-time slice identification and segregation at the packet-processing
stage, supporting a large number of heterogeneous slices.
The prototype
demonstrated deterministic processing with a latency of 2 clock cycles per
packet, independent of the slice configuration.
The theoretical analysis showed that, for a bandwidth of 100 MHz, up
to 3822 slices may coexist within a single slot when each PRB-symbol tuple
is treated as an independent slice. This scenario stresses memory indexing
and lookup structures and validates the scalability limits of the proposed
design. Experimental evaluation under mMTC and URLLC configurations
confirmed the system’s capability to handle both high slice density and strin-
gent latency constraints. In particular, memory-occupancy analysis revealed
that more than 5 % of the available BRAM resources were required for slice
management, while parallel list structures consumed up to 48.94 % of the
LUTs resources in larger configurations. These results highlight the inher-
ent trade-off between scalability and hardware cost in disaggregated RAN
architectures.
34


From a practical deployment perspective, the results indicate that imple-
menting slicing enforcement at the O-RU level is feasible but requires careful
dimensioning of memory structures and parallel processing units. The design
choices directly impact FPGA resource utilization and may constrain the in-
tegration of additional O-RU functionalities. Therefore, slicing support in
disaggregated architectures must be co-designed with hardware constraints
rather than treated as a purely logical function.
Future work includes integrating with the SMO to expose real-time met-
rics (e.g., FIFO occupancy and slice processing latency), enabling closed-loop
optimization via RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC)-based control. Further
validation in network simulators (e.g., NS-3) and integration with commer-
cial O-RUs will allow assessment of the Slice Agent under realistic traffic and
deployment conditions.

However, uplink slicing iden- tification in shared Open-RUs (O-RUs) presents a fundamental challenge because the Open-DU (O-DU) handles scheduling, and the O-RU does not inherently know which uplink data belongs to which slice. Our design em- ploys a pipeline architecture with dedicated paths for time-sensitive, flexible slicing, enabling slice isolation and prioritization.
